extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, law students, and judges (U.S. patent litigation practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Enumerates and explains the principal defenses available to defendants in U.S. patent infringement suits (procedural, substantive, and title-based objections), with doctrinal nuance and case citations. Focused on how and when each defence operates and when it may be cured (re-issue, disclaimer, government action, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defence of public use and sale (two years) / prior use
rubrics_metrics.description: That the defence of public use and sale more than two years before the invention is not known to our law; under the defence of two years' public use the defence of prior use cannot be made, nor is it sustained by evidence of a prior patent without the plaintiff's knowledge over two years before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: Belleher v. Darling (1878), Myers v. Busby (1887), Parks v. Booth (1880). The text indicates limitations on using prior public use/sale and prior patent evidence as a defense under the 'two years' statutory framework; nuances and historical authorities are provided. (Context: appears as part of earlier defenses addressing statutory bars and prior user/patent issues.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Ninth Defence: Issuance not in conformity with law
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial that the patent, though actually issued by the government, was issued in accordance with the formal requirements of the law (i.e., Patent Office disregarded legal methods or acted beyond jurisdiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains which procedural omissions are cured by allowance (omission of oath or fee, absence of attestations, trivial irregularities) and which are reviewable (false oath/suggestion, missing signatures or seal, departure from the application, patent issued to wrong person, issuance without required notice to a pending caveator). Re-issue issued to correct voluntary defects may transcend Office jurisdiction and be invalid; fraud by government officials generally can be attacked only by the United States. Case citations and cross-references (§§ 428, 451, 617, 620, 714, 1016, etc.) illustrate distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenth Defence: Invention not legally patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial that the invention covered by the patent is patentable subject-matter under the laws of the United States (i.e., the claimed subject does not fall within the statutory classes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguished from other objections (e.g., lack of inventive act). When the defect is apparent on the face of the patent, courts may judicially notice it without formal pleading. (Short discussion noting similarity to the fourth defence but directed to statutory subject-matter.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Eleventh Defence: Fraudulent concealment or misrepresentation in specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial that the patentee or his assignor acted in good faith in disclosing the invention in the specification — that the description was made to contain less than the whole truth or more than necessary to produce deception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essence is fraudulent intent. Ambiguities from inability to describe do not constitute this defence. A specification designed to mislead skilled persons (prevent full use or force disadvantage) forfeits the patentee's rights and, if established by sufficient evidence, renders the patent void. Historical authorities and notes cited; differences drawn between intentional fraud (permanent penalty) and innocent ambiguity (potentially curable by re-issue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Twelfth Defence: Ambiguity / insufficiency of description (enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Averment that the description in the specification is insufficient to enable persons skilled in the art to make and use the invention without exercise of their own inventive skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law requires a written description sufficiently full, clear, concise, and exact to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the invention. The Patent Office's allowance is reviewable in court in infringement cases. The treatise discusses the debate whether only fraudulent insufficiency invalidates a patent, concluding that inability of skilled persons to practice the invention from the description alone invalidates the patent (i.e., lack of enablement is a complete defence). Authorities, statutory references (§§ 41, 42, 481, 488–494, etc.), and policy reasoning (the patent contract and public consideration) are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thirteenth Defence: Excessive claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Averment that the claims are excessive and include matter open to the public or derived from others; intentional over-claiming to appropriate public domain is an attempt to defraud and forfeits rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If excessive claims were inserted inadvertently (no wilful default) they may be cured by re-issue or disclaimer when the remaining matter is a material, separable part of the original invention and amendment is made without unreasonable delay. If excessive claims are intentional, not amendable without eliminating patentable subject-matter, or not timely amended, the defence is proper and will defeat the suit. If amendment is made during suit, plaintiff may recover on amended claim but may be denied costs. Cross-references to procedures for disclaimer and re-issue (§§ 642–658, 687, 651, etc.) and case law illustrate the rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourteenth Defence: Ambiguity / indefiniteness in the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial that the claim defines the invention with sufficient precision and completeness to distinguish it from other inventions — i.e., claim is ambiguous, uncertain, or unintelligible, rendering the patent void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claim is 'the life of the patent' and must clearly draw the line of monopoly. If a claim conveys no idea, is uncertain about essential characteristics, or expresses multiple inventions leaving the intended scope doubtful, it is inoperative. In multi-claim patents, defective claims do not invalidate other sufficient claims; each claim stands or falls on its own. Authorities and examples are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fifteenth Defence: Surrender of the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Averment that the patent, though once valid, has been surrendered and all rights of action extinguished (e.g., surrendered for re-issue or abandoned to the public).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concedes prior lawful issuance but asserts extinguishment by surrender. Expiration by lapse of term does not affect accrued causes of action. Defence is available whether surrender occurred before or after suit. Case references provided (e.g., Moffitt v. Gaar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sixteenth Defence: Repeal (annulment) of the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Averment that the patent never lawfully existed or has been recalled/cancelled by the government (i.e., rescinded or annulled and thus void ab initio).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs where a rival inventor obtains revocation or the government prevails in suit to repeal; when held void ab initio, apparent rights under it never existed. Defence applies in suits based on such a patent; if annulment affected only certain owners/territories, it may not bar actions by unaffected owners. Cross-references to related sections and cases are included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seventeenth Defence: Lack of legal title in plaintiff
rubrics_metrics.description: Attack on the plaintiff's title — denial that plaintiff holds such legal interest (patentee, assignee, or lawful grantee) as to maintain an action at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At law, only legal owners (patentee, assignee, or territorial grantee) can sue for infringement. Equitable interests generally cannot be used to defeat the record owner's claims in an action at law. Capacity/organizational defects (corporate incapacity) are matters of abatement rather than this defence. Authorities cited (e.g., Dental Vulcanite Co. v. Wetherbee).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eighteenth Defence: Non-coverage of defendant's art (non-infringement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial that the art or instrument employed by the defendant is covered by the patent (i.e., assertion that the defendant's product/process does not fall within the scope of the patent claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduces the non-infringement line of defence; further elaboration appears subsequently in the treatise. (In context this is the beginning of the group of defences attacking whether the defendant's practice is within the claimed monopoly.)
